mainTopic: Who swears in a dispute over an agreed wage (שמואל, רבי יהודה and the חכמים), and the robbed person's oath
overview: The amud opens by finishing an earlier point: both clauses of a ברייתא about a hired worker need proof, but it only mentions proof that makes the employer pay. Then רב's students ask שמואל who swears when a craftsman says the agreed wage was two coins and the employer says one. שמואל rules that the employer swears, because people remember the wage they agreed on. רב נחמן defends this against a ברייתא of רבה בר שמואל. A second ברייתא, about a cloak, lets the craftsman swear and collect. רב נחמן בר יצחק answers that this ברייתא follows רבי יהודה, and the גמרא finds the source in another ברייתא. רב שישא objects that the חכמים should agree with רבי יהודה here. רבא explains that the two sides differ in principle: רבי יהודה does not make a fix on top of a fix, while the חכמים hold that an agreed price is remembered. The amud then turns to the משנה's case of a robbed person, explaining that the witnesses saw him actually take small items hidden under his clothes. רב יהודה begins a related ruling that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Both clauses need proof, but only proof that leads to payment is mentioned
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that both parts of the earlier ברייתא involve proof. The ברייתא only spells out proof that makes the employer pay, not proof that leads to an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: Both the first and last parts of the ברייתא involve proof. It only mentions proof that makes someone pay; it does not mention proof that leads to an oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is answering a question from the end of the previous amud: why does only one clause of the ברייתא mention proof? It says both clauses really need proof, but only one kind of proof gets mentioned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even in the first clause, the worker needs witnesses that he was hired before he can swear and collect. The ברייתא skips that because it only mentions proof that directly makes the employer pay. Proof that only opens the door to an oath is left unsaid.

keyTerms.meaning: The first clause of a teaching
The last clause of a teaching

phrases.english: Both the first clause and the last clause involve proof;
it teaches proof that makes him pay,
but proof that leads to an oath, it does not teach.
phrases.notes: Witnesses that only let the worker swear are also needed, but the ברייתא doesn't bother saying so.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers a question raised before this section about the wording of a ברייתא on a hired worker.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the wording: both clauses require proof, but only proof that leads to payment is stated.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only the clause that mentions proof actually needs proof.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both clauses need proof. The ברייתא only states the kind of proof that obligates payment.

steps.title: רב's students ask שמואל: who swears in a dispute over the agreed wage?
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה בר אבא reports that the students in רב's study hall sent שמואל a question. When a craftsman claims two coins were agreed and the employer says one, who takes the oath?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה בר אבא said: They sent a question to שמואל from רב's study hall: 'Teach us, our teacher. A craftsman says, "You set my wage at two," and the other says, "I only set it at one." Who swears?'
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. The students in רב's study hall ask שמואל how to rule when a craftsman and an employer disagree about the wage they agreed on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the employer would swear to deny part of a claim. But חז"ל set up a special rule that lets a hired worker swear and collect. The question is whether that special rule also covers a dispute over the amount agreed, or only over whether he was paid at all.

keyTerms.meaning: They sent to him (a question by message)
From the study hall of רב
Let our teacher instruct us (a respectful way to ask)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba said:
They sent to Shmuel from the study hall of Rav:
Let our teacher instruct us:
A craftsman says: 'You fixed two for me,'
and the other one says:
'I fixed only one for you' —
who takes the oath?

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַחוּ לֵיהּ מִבֵּי רַב לִשְׁמוּאֵל: יְלַמְּדֵנוּ רַבֵּינוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic: a dispute over the agreed wage.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: In a dispute over the agreed wage, does the craftsman swear and collect, or does the employer swear?

steps.title: שמואל: the employer swears, because people remember the wage they agreed on
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rules that the employer swears and the craftsman loses the extra amount. The reason is that people clearly remember what wage they set.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: In this case the employer swears and the craftsman loses, because people certainly remember the wage they agreed on.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל answers the question. The employer takes the oath, and the craftsman does not get the second coin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The special rule letting a worker swear and collect assumes the busy employer may have forgotten whether he paid. An agreed wage is something people remember well, so there is no worry that the employer forgot. The usual rule applies: the defendant swears and keeps his money.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ruling of שמואל is the base text that the rest of the section challenges and defends.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶן: בְּזוֹ יִשָּׁבַע בַּעַל הַבַּיִת,
phrases.english: He said to them: In this case the employer swears,
and the craftsman loses;
the fixing of wages, people certainly remember.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶן: בְּזוֹ יִשָּׁבַע בַּעַל הַבַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question sent from רב's study hall.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The employer swears and the craftsman loses, since people remember an agreed wage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a dispute over the agreed wage, the employer swears and the craftsman loses the difference.

steps.title: Challenge from רבה בר שמואל's ברייתא: no oath is mentioned
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר שמואל's ברייתא says that in a dispute over the agreed wage, the craftsman must bring proof or he gets nothing. It does not mention an oath by the employer, which seems to clash with שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רבה בר שמואל taught: If there is a dispute about the agreed wage, the one claiming money must bring proof, and if he doesn't, his claim is dropped. Why? Let the employer swear, and then the craftsman should lose!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions שמואל's ruling. A ברייתא seems to say the craftsman simply loses without proof, with no oath from the employer at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל said the employer must swear before the craftsman loses. The ברייתא says the craftsman's claim simply drops if he has no proof. The גמרא asks why the ברייתא leaves out the employer's oath.

keyTerms.meaning: One who wants to take money from another must bring proof
It is dropped / his claim falls away

phrases.aramaic: אִינִי?! וְהָא תָּנֵי רַבָּה בַּר שְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: Is that so? But didn't Rabba bar Shmuel teach:
If he fixed a wage, the one who takes from his fellow must bring proof,
phrases.notes: He means a case where they argue over the agreed wage. The craftsman is the one trying to take money.

phrases.english: and if he does not bring proof, his claim is dropped.
Why? Let the employer swear,
and then the craftsman loses!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי?! וְהָא תָּנֵי רַבָּה בַּר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שמואל's ruling in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling that the employer swears and only then the craftsman loses.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says the craftsman's claim drops without proof and mentions no oath, so it seems the employer does not need to swear.

steps.title: רב נחמן: the ברייתא lists two options
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן explains that the ברייתא gives two possible outcomes. Either the craftsman brings proof and collects, or the employer swears and the craftsman loses.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: The ברייתא is teaching two sides. Either the craftsman brings proof and collects, or the employer swears and the craftsman loses.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן defends שמואל. The words 'his claim is dropped' are short for: if there is no proof, the employer swears and the craftsman loses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא did not mean the craftsman loses with no oath at all. It was only contrasting the two paths: proof wins the claim, and without proof the employer swears. So the ברייתא fits שמואל after all.

keyTerms.meaning: It teaches two separate sides / options

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said: It teaches two sides —
either he brings proof and collects,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ יִשָּׁבַע בַּעַל הַבַּיִת וְיַפְסִיד אוּמָּן.
phrases.english: or the employer swears and the craftsman loses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the ברייתא as listing two alternatives.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'His claim is dropped' means he loses without any oath from the employer.
steps.terutzMaskana: Without proof the employer swears, then the craftsman loses, just as שמואל said.

steps.title: Challenge from the ברייתא of the cloak given to a craftsman
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that while the craftsman still holds the cloak, the owner must bring proof. If the craftsman returned it and they argue on time, he swears and collects. If the time has passed, he must bring proof. That he swears and collects seems to go against שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: Someone gives his cloak to a craftsman. The craftsman says, 'You set my wage at two,' and the owner says, 'I only set it at one.' As long as the cloak is with the craftsman, the owner must bring proof. If he gave it back on time, the craftsman swears and collects. If the time passed, the one taking money from the other must bring proof.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא that seems to argue with שמואל. Step 7 pinpoints the clash, and step 8 gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case is exactly שמואל's case: a dispute over the agreed wage. Yet the ברייתא says that if the cloak was returned on time, the craftsman swears and collects. שמואל said the employer swears, because people remember agreed wages.
steps.confusionAlert: The middle case (returned on time, the craftsman swears and collects) is what clashes with שמואל. While the craftsman still holds the cloak, the owner needs proof because the craftsman is holding the item.

phrases.english: They challenged: One who gives his cloak to a craftsman,
the craftsman says: 'You fixed two for me,'

phrases.aramaic: וְהַלָּה אוֹמֵר: ״לֹא קָצַצְתִּי לְךָ אֶלָּא אֶחָת״;
phrases.english: and the other says: 'I fixed only one for you';
as long as the cloak is in the craftsman's hand,
it is upon the owner to bring proof.
If he gave it to him in its time, he swears and collects.
phrases.notes: 'In its time' means on the day he returned the cloak. The one who swears here is the craftsman.

phrases.aramaic: עָבַר זְמַנּוֹ – הַמּוֹצִיא מֵחֲבֵרוֹ עָלָיו הָרְאָיָה.
phrases.english: If its time passed, the one who takes from his fellow must bring proof.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first challenge was answered, the גמרא brings a second challenge to שמואל.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling that the employer swears in a dispute over the agreed wage.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says that when the cloak is returned on time, the craftsman swears and collects, the opposite of שמואל's ruling.

steps.title: Why does the craftsman swear instead of the employer?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא spells out the attack. The ברייתא says the craftsman swears and collects, but according to שמואל the employer should swear and the craftsman should lose.
steps.simpleTranslation: In any case, the ברייתא says that when they argue on time, the craftsman swears and collects. Why? According to שמואל, the employer should swear and the craftsman should lose.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing the question it began in the last step. It points to the one line in the ברייתא that does not fit שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל said the employer swears, because people remember what wage they set. The ברייתא gives the oath to the craftsman, and he walks away with the money. That is the exact opposite result.

keyTerms.meaning: In its time: the claim is made before the payment deadline has passed
In any case, at least (this part)
Swears and collects: the claimant takes an oath and gets paid
And the craftsman loses (the disputed amount)

phrases.english: In any event, in its time he swears and collects;
phrases.notes: The גמרא is focusing on just this one clause of the ברייתא from the last step: the craftsman who returned the cloak and argues on time.

phrases.english: Why?
Let the employer swear and the craftsman lose!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge from the ברייתא quoted in step 6 by naming exactly where it clashes with שמואל.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling that the employer swears and the craftsman loses
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא gives the oath to the craftsman and lets him collect, while שמואל gives the oath to the employer.

steps.title: The ברייתא follows רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק says the ברייתא follows רבי יהודה. He holds that whenever the oath would normally fall on the employer, the worker swears and collects instead.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: Whose view is this? It is רבי יהודה's. He says that any time the oath leans toward the employer, the hired worker swears and collects.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק answers the question. The ברייתא is not the view everyone holds; it follows רבי יהודה, and שמואל follows the other חכמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the employer admits part of the claim: 'I agreed to one coin.' Normally that would make the employer the one who swears. רבי יהודה says that in such a case the oath is moved to the worker, who swears and collects. שמואל can simply follow the חכמים who disagree with this.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבי יהודה says the employer never swears. He says that in the case where the employer would normally swear, the חכמים moved the oath over to the worker.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
Whose is this? It is Rabbi Yehuda's,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר: כׇּל זְמַן שֶׁשְּׁבוּעָה נוֹטָה אֵצֶל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת –
phrases.english: who says: any time that an oath leans toward the employer,
phrases.notes: He means a case where the employer admits part of the claim, so the oath would normally be his.

phrases.english: the hired worker swears and collects.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 7 by tying the ברייתא to one specific תנא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attribution: the source follows one opinion (רבי יהודה), and שמואל follows the other side
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to be everyone's view, so it would contradict שמואל.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is רבי יהודה's, and שמואל agrees with the חכמים who disagree with him.

steps.title: Which statement of רבי יהודה is meant?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where רבי יהודה says this. It cannot be his statement in the משנה, because there he makes the worker's oath harder to get, not easier.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which רבי יהודה? If you say the רבי יהודה of the משנה, he is being strict there. We learned: רבי יהודה says the worker does not swear and collect unless there is a partial admission.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא checks the source of רב נחמן בר יצחק's claim. It tests the obvious candidate, the משנה, and shows it does not fit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the חכמים let a worker swear and collect quite broadly. רבי יהודה comes to limit this: only when the employer admits part. That statement is strict toward the worker, while רב נחמן בר יצחק needs a רבי יהודה who gives the worker an oath. So the משנה is not the right source.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (introduces a possibility the גמרא will reject)
Partial admission: the defendant admits part of the claim

phrases.english: Which Rabbi Yehuda?
If you say the Rabbi Yehuda of the משנה,
phrases.notes: This is the משנה on דף מד ע״ב about a worker who swears and collects.

phrases.english: he is being strict!
phrases.notes: Strict toward the worker. He limits when the worker gets to swear.

phrases.english: As we learned: Rabbi Yehuda says:
Not unless there is partial admission there!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵי רַבִּי יְהוּדָה? אִילֵימָא רַבִּי יְהוּדָה דְּמַתְנִיתִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks where the רבי יהודה cited in step 8 comes from, and rejects the משנה as the source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which teaching of רבי יהודה supports the idea that the worker swears where the oath leans toward the employer?

steps.title: It is רבי יהודה in a ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The source is a ברייתא. A hired worker swears and collects while his time has not passed, and רבי יהודה says this applies when the employer admits part of the claim.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is the רבי יהודה of a ברייתא. A hired worker, as long as his time has not passed, swears and collects. If his time has passed, he does not swear and collect. רבי יהודה said: When is this? When he said, 'Give me my fifty dinar wages that you hold,' and the employer says, 'You already received a gold dinar of it.' Or when he said, 'You set two,' and the other says, 'I set only one.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question by quoting a ברייתא. In it, רבי יהודה describes the very case of 'you set two, I set only one' as one where the worker swears and collects.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both of רבי יהודה's examples, the employer admits part of the claim. That is exactly the 'oath leans toward the employer' situation, and the worker still swears and collects. This matches the cloak ברייתא, so it fits רבי יהודה, not the חכמים whom שמואל follows.

keyTerms.meaning: Of a ברייתא: a teaching from the time of the משנה that is not in the משנה itself
His time has passed: the deadline for paying wages is over
When? (introduces a limit on the rule)
A gold dinar, worth 25 silver dinars

steps.whatToRemember: The worker swearing and collecting in a wage-amount argument follows רבי יהודה's ברייתא, where the employer admits part. שמואל, who has the employer swear, follows the חכמים.

phrases.english: Rather, the Rabbi Yehuda of a ברייתא,
as it is taught: A hired worker,

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל זְמַן שֶׁלֹּא עָבַר עָלָיו זְמַנּוֹ –
phrases.english: as long as his time has not passed,
he swears and collects;
and if not, he does not swear and collect.
And Rabbi Yehuda said: When is this?
When he said to him:
'Give me my wages of fifty dinar
that I have in your hand';
and he says: 'You received a gold dinar of them,'
phrases.notes: A gold dinar equals 25 silver ones, so the employer is admitting he still owes half.

phrases.english: or he said to him: 'You set two,'

phrases.aramaic: וְהַלָּה אוֹמֵר: ״לֹא קָצַצְתִּי לְךָ אֶלָּא אֶחָת״;
phrases.english: and the other says: 'I set for you only one';

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 9 by giving the correct source for רבי יהודה's view.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי יהודה's view is found in a ברייתא. There he says the worker swears and collects when the employer admits part, including the case of 'you set two, I set only one.'

steps.title: End of רבי יהודה's ברייתא: if the employer denies everything, the worker needs proof
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא of רבי יהודה ends. If the employer says 'I never hired you' or 'I already paid you,' the worker gets no oath and must bring proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if the employer said, 'I never hired you,' or 'I hired you and already paid you,' then the one who wants to take money from his friend must bring proof.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting the ברייתא from the last step. It shows the cases where, according to רבי יהודה, the worker does NOT get to swear and collect.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the last step, רבי יהודה said the worker swears and collects only when the employer admits part of the claim. Here he spells out the other side. If the employer denies the whole thing, the normal rule returns: the one trying to take money must prove it.

keyTerms.meaning: I never hired you, a full denial
I already gave you your wages
The one who wants to take money from another must bring proof

phrases.english: But if he said to him: 'I never hired you,'

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ: ״שְׂכַרְתִּיךָ וְנָתַתִּי לְךָ שְׂכָרֶךָ״ –
phrases.english: or he said to him: 'I hired you and I gave you your wages' –
the one who takes money from his fellow must bring the proof.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא begun in step 10 by giving the cases where רבי יהודה denies the worker an oath.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי יהודה lets the worker swear and collect only when the employer admits part of the claim. When the employer denies everything, the worker must bring proof.

steps.title: רב שישא asks: how can the agreed-price case follow only רבי יהודה?
steps.stepSummary: רב שישא בריה דרב אידי asks how the ברייתא about an agreed price can follow only רבי יהודה. The חכמים are kinder to the worker than רבי יהודה, so they should agree too.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שישא son of רב אידי objected: Is the agreed-price case really only רבי יהודה and not the חכמים? Look: where רבי יהודה is strict, the חכמים are lenient. So where רבי יהודה is lenient, would the חכמים be strict?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב שישא attacks רב נחמן בר יצחק's answer from step 8. That answer said the craftsman ברייתא follows only רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, רבי יהודה is the strict one. He limits when the worker may swear, while the חכמים give the worker an oath more often. So if רבי יהודה lets the worker swear in the agreed-price case, the more generous חכמים should surely agree. It makes no sense to say they would turn strict here.

keyTerms.meaning: He objected to it, raising a strong challenge
He agreed on a price, the case of arguing over the agreed wage

phrases.aramaic: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב שִׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי:
phrases.english: Rav Sheisha son of Rav Idi objected to it:
But the case of 'he agreed on a price' –
is it Rabbi Yehuda and not the Rabbis?!
Now, where Rabbi Yehuda is strict –
the Rabbis are lenient,
so where Rabbi Yehuda is lenient –
would the Rabbis be strict?!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב שִׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the source just found for רבי יהודה to challenge the answer of step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן בר יצחק's claim that the craftsman ברייתא follows only רבי יהודה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The חכמים give the worker an oath more often than רבי יהודה does. So any case where רבי יהודה lets the worker swear should be accepted by the חכמים too, all the more so.

steps.title: But it cannot be the חכמים either, or רבה בר שמואל's ברייתא fits no one
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back. If the agreed-price ברייתא follows the חכמים too, then the ברייתא of רבה בר שמואל, which says the worker needs proof in that case, matches neither side.
steps.simpleTranslation: So what will you say, that it follows the חכמים? Then whose view is the ברייתא taught by רבה בר שמואל: 'If he agreed on a price, the one taking money must bring proof'? It is neither רבי יהודה nor the חכמים!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that רב שישא's objection creates its own problem. If both sides let the worker swear in the agreed-price case, another ברייתא has no one to follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה בר שמואל taught that in the agreed-price case the worker gets no oath and must bring proof. If רבי יהודה and the חכמים both let the worker swear there, that ברייתא matches no one. So we cannot simply say both sides agree. Some real difference between them must exist.

keyTerms.meaning: So what will you say instead?

phrases.english: So what, then: the Rabbis?

phrases.aramaic: וְאֶלָּא הָא דְּתָנֵי רַבָּה בַּר שְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: But then that which Rabba bar Shmuel taught:
'If he agreed on a price, the one who takes from his fellow must bring the proof,'
whose view is it?
Neither Rabbi Yehuda nor the Rabbis!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Pushes back against רב שישא's objection by showing that his suggestion leaves רבה בר שמואל's ברייתא with no one to follow. This does not settle the matter; רבא's 'אלא' in step 14 gives the real resolution.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that the חכמים must agree with רבי יהודה in the agreed-price case.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: If both sides let the worker swear when he agreed on a price, the ברייתא of רבה בר שמואל, which requires proof, matches no one.

steps.title: רבא: רבי יהודה limits the worker's oath because we do not add a fix on top of a fix
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains the real reason for רבי יהודה's view. The חכמים made a special fix for the worker only where the employer's oath would be from the Torah. Where that oath is itself rabbinic, we do not add another fix on top of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: This is what they argue about. רבי יהודה holds: where the oath is from the Torah, they made a special fix for the hired worker. But where the oath is rabbinic, that oath is already a fix, and we do not make a fix on top of a fix.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers רב שישא's objection. He explains that רבי יהודה is not simply 'stricter' than the חכמים. His view comes from a different principle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the employer admits part of the claim, the Torah would make him swear. The חכמים moved that oath over to the worker so he could swear and collect. When the employer denies everything, his oath is only rabbinic, so it is already a fix. רבי יהודה says we do not change an existing fix with another fix, so the worker gets no oath there. This is why the two sides do not line up as simply 'lenient' and 'strict.'

keyTerms.meaning: This is what they argue about
A fix, a rule the חכמים made
We do not make a fix on top of a fix

steps.whatToRemember: For רבי יהודה, the worker swears and collects only where the employer's oath would have been from the Torah, meaning he admitted part of the claim. When the employer denies everything, his oath is only rabbinic, and we do not stack one fix on top of another.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't read this as 'רבי יהודה is just stricter with workers.' רבא's whole point is that his limit comes from a principle, no fix on top of a fix, and not from a general strictness.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule 'תקנתא לתקנתא לא עבדינן' is a general principle about rabbinic fixes, and it explains the shape of רבי יהודה's view.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
This is what they argue about –
Rabbi Yehuda holds: with a Torah-level oath –
phrases.notes: He means the employer's oath when he admits part of the claim. That oath comes from the Torah.

phrases.english: they made a special fix for the hired worker;
but with a rabbinic oath, it is already a fix,
phrases.notes: This is the oath when the employer denies everything. That oath is only rabbinic.

phrases.english: and we do not make a fix on top of a fix.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a new account of the argument that answers רב שישא's objection in step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the argument: רבי יהודה's limit comes from a principle, not from general strictness.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought רבי יהודה was simply stricter with workers than the חכמים, so the חכמים should agree whenever he is lenient.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יהודה lets the worker swear only in place of a Torah oath. A rabbinic oath is already a fix, and we do not add a fix on top of a fix.

steps.title: The רבנן help the worker even for a rabbinic oath, but not in a dispute over the agreed price
steps.stepSummary: רבא finishes his answer. The רבנן help the worker even where the employer's oath is rabbinic. But in a dispute over the agreed price, the employer remembers the amount, so no special help is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן hold that even where the employer's oath is only rabbinic, we still make a special fix for the worker. But when they argue about the agreed price, the employer surely remembers it, so he swears and is free.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רבא's answer by explaining how the רבנן see things differently from רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב שישא assumed the רבנן are simply 'kinder' to the worker in every case. רבא shows they use a different measure. They help the worker even where the employer's oath is rabbinic, but only where the employer might really be confused. Once the price was agreed on, the employer remembers it. This is why the ברייתא of רבה בר שמואל, which says the worker needs proof, fits the רבנן.

keyTerms.meaning: The agreed-upon price for the work
A rule that comes from the Rabbis, not from the Torah

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהודה and the רבנן do not argue about who is kinder to the worker. רבי יהודה gives the special fix only where the employer's oath would be from the Torah. The רבנן give it even for a rabbinic oath, but not in a dispute over the agreed price, because the employer remembers that.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the רבנן are 'stricter' here. They help the worker in more kinds of oath cases, yet they hold back in the agreed-price case for a separate reason: the employer remembers.
steps.whyThisMatters: This answers רב שישא's challenge. Both ברייתות now fit, each with a different side.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis hold:
with a rabbinic oath also
we make a special fix for the hired worker,
but the agreed price, he surely remembers.
phrases.notes: 'He' is the employer. Because he remembers the agreed price, he swears and is free, and the worker does not get to swear.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רבא's answer from step 14 by giving the רבנן's side.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows that the two sides use different measures, not more or less kindness
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The רבנן help the worker in every case where רבי יהודה does, and more.
steps.terutzMaskana: The רבנן help the worker even where the employer's oath is rabbinic. In a dispute over the agreed price, the employer remembers the amount, so no fix is needed.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: the case of the robbed person
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of the נגזל. Witnesses saw a man enter another person's house to take collateral.
steps.simpleTranslation: How does it work for someone who was robbed? Witnesses testified that the man entered his house to take collateral from him, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new topic by quoting the next case in the משנה. This sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the robbed person swears and collects. This is because witnesses saw the other man go into his house to take collateral without permission. The גמרא quotes this so it can examine how strong that testimony really is.

phrases.english: The robbed person, how so?
Witnesses were testifying about him
that he entered his house to take collateral from him, etc.
phrases.notes: 'Etc.' means the rest of the משנה: the owner says 'you took my things,' the other man denies it, and the owner swears and collects.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the worker's case to the next case in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When witnesses saw a man enter a house to take collateral, the owner swears about what was taken and collects.

steps.title: Maybe he never took anything: people threaten without acting
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the משנה. Seeing him go in to take collateral does not prove he took any. רב נחמן teaches that a person who threatens to cut down a tree is not assumed to have done it.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe he did not take collateral? Didn't רב נחמן say: if someone holds an axe and says 'I'll go cut down so-and-so's palm tree,' and the tree is found cut down and lying there, we do not say he cut it down? So people often threaten and don't act. Here too, maybe he threatened and didn't act!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how the owner can collect when the witnesses only saw the man's plan, not the taking itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן's case is strong. The man had an axe, said what he would do, and the tree really was cut down, yet we still do not blame him. If even that is not proof, then merely walking in 'to take collateral' surely does not prove he took anything.

keyTerms.meaning: He threatens but does not act

phrases.english: But perhaps he did not take collateral from him?
Didn't רב נחמן say:
one who holds an axe in his hand,
and says: 'I will go and cut down'
'so-and-so's palm tree,'
and it is found cut down and lying on the ground,
we do not say that he cut it down?
So we see a person tends
to threaten and not do it,
here too, he threatened and did not do it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the evidence in the משנה that was just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's assumption that witnesses who saw him enter 'to take collateral' are enough for the owner to swear and collect.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב נחמן shows that a stated plan, even with the result found later, does not prove the act. So entering with a plan to take collateral proves nothing.

steps.title: Read the משנה as: and he did take collateral
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה means the witnesses saw him actually take collateral.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say: 'and he took collateral from him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by reading the משנה's words differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The witnesses did not see only a plan. They saw him enter and actually take things. So the problem of 'threatening without doing' no longer applies.

keyTerms.meaning: And he took collateral from him

phrases.english: Say: 'and he took collateral from him.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the wording of the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The witnesses saw only his plan to take collateral.
steps.terutzMaskana: The witnesses saw him actually take collateral.

steps.title: Then let the witnesses say what he took
steps.stepSummary: If the witnesses saw him take things, they can tell us what he took, so why does the owner need to swear?
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let us see what he took as collateral!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes on the new answer. If the witnesses saw the taking, they should know what was taken.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner swears in the משנה because the amount is unclear. But if eyewitnesses watched him take the items, they could just describe them. Then no oath would be needed.

phrases.english: Then let us see what he took as collateral?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for the owner's oath once the witnesses saw the taking.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Eyewitnesses to the taking could tell the court what was taken, so the oath is not needed.

steps.title: The items were small enough to hide under his clothes
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that the owner claims small items that could be carried hidden under his garments, so the witnesses could not see what they were.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: it is where the owner claims items that can be carried under one's garments.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question of why the witnesses can't simply say what was taken.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The witnesses saw him take something, but it was hidden under his clothes. So they cannot say exactly what or how much it was. Since the owner's claim is believable, he swears and collects.

keyTerms.meaning: Under the flaps of his clothing

steps.whatToRemember: The robbed person swears and collects only when witnesses saw the man actually take things. The items must also be small enough to hide under his clothes, so the witnesses could not see exactly what was taken.

phrases.english: רבה בר בר חנה said,
רבי יוחנן said:
where he claims against him items
that can be carried under his garments.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה, אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 19.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The witnesses could see exactly what was taken.
steps.terutzMaskana: The items were hidden under his clothes, so the witnesses could not tell what they were.

steps.title: רב יהודה begins: someone seen hiding items under his clothes
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה starts a related ruling about a person seen hiding items under his garments and leaving. His ruling continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: if they saw him hide items under his garments and leave,
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling from רב יהודה on a similar topic. This line only sets up the case, and his ruling comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This builds on the idea of items 'under his garments' from רבי יוחנן. רב יהודה describes witnesses who saw a man hide items and walk out. The question of what the law is in this case is answered in the continuation.

phrases.english: רב יהודה said:
if they saw him hide items
under his garments and leave,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: רָאוּהוּ שֶׁהִטְמִין כֵּלִים תַּחַת כְּנָפָיו וְיָצָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a related case about hidden items, following רבי יוחנן's answer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The case is set up here: a man was seen hiding items under his garments and leaving. רב יהודה's ruling comes in the continuation.
